newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Yield Spreads-Bloc in rates shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Australia Yield Spreads-Bloc in rates shake-up.

text.p: Dollar bloc yield differentials saw a shake-up on Friday in the aftermath of a surprise rate hike by the Bank of Canada and a larger than expected policy loosening endorsement by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.
And further volatility in the bloc is expected next week with the Reserve Bank of Australia holding its board meeting on July 1 and the Federal Open Market Committee on July 1 and 2.

Hopes of an easing by the RBA in current 5.5 percent official interest rates remain, although the market has watered its over enthusiasm for such a move in the past few days, while the jury remains out on a Fed tightening this time round.

Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia, believes that out of this shuffling of interest rates, Australian debt could benefit from switching next week because the local economy still has excess capacity, putting it in a favourable position internationally.

"We still have scope for spread compression against U.S. Treasuries, I think we will still get some switching out of Canada into Australia next week, and I wouldn't be surprised that the New Zealand rally has gone too far," Roberts added.

Australian spreads to Canada tightened sharply after the Bank of Canada hiked its key bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent, its first rate rise since February 1995, and citing the recent weakness in the Canadian dollar for the move.
PaineWebber International (U.K.) expects the BOC will have to tighten policy again as technical factors for the Canadian dollar are very poor.

In contrast, it expects the Australian dollar to benefit from rising commodity prices and should not come under untoward pressure against the U.S. dollar even though there is an RBA easing bias, it said in a report.

"Switches out of (Canada), especially out of the short end, into Australia, should reap benefits, particularly given a further Canadian rate hike is likely due to C$ weakness, which is expected to persist," PaineWebber's James McKay said.
Meanwhile, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand endorsed a 100 basis points easing from its policy projections in March, larger than the New Zealand market had already priced in.

Australian yield differentials widened on the news and the 10-year spread to New Zealand confirmed Thursday's break into positive territory after the N.Z. budget, although this had been largely due to a sell-off locally.

"People will like the middle to shorter end of the New Zealand curve. The long end has had a good rally, but it is a bit problematic now because of the budget," said UBS' Roberts, who saw the debut coalition budget primarily focussed on spending.
